summary: Redwood AE + SE walked Atlas Health through the Console tracing, error analysis, and request logs flows. Demo focused on finding slow requests, correlating traces with request logs, identifying a model fallback causing tokenization errors, and showing RBAC/audit log features. Next steps: send SOC2 + arch docs, run benchmark, schedule pilot kickoff.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-05-12 16:00 PDT | Duration: ~45m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Rachel K. (Atlas Eng Manager), Omar P. (Atlas SRE), Sophia L. (Atlas SecOps)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, really appreciate you carving the time, we'll do a quick walkthrough of the Redwood Console tracing and request logs, show how to debug slow requests and errors. Liam will drive the demo.
[00:18] Rachel: sounds good, we mainly want to see correlation between traces and the raw request logs - our SREs keep getting a few 500s and some timeouts.
[00:28] Liam: got it, and if at any point you want me to dig into the backend view or show the KV cache hits, just interrupt.
[00:35] Omar: quick note - we care about PII redaction and retention policies. Also we use SAML SSO and have a pinned VPC for Dedicated later.
[00:45] Maya: yeah we'll point out RBAC, audit logs, and the private deployment considerations.

[01:02] Liam: ok starting screen share, this is the Console home, then I go to Observability -> Traces. Here you can see a list of traces by timestamp, latency, and error rate. Notice the search bar supports request_id and model_id filters.
[01:28] Rachel: is request_id the same as the one in our app logs? We can send one sample.
[01:35] Liam: yes if you pass x-request-id we surface it and correlate automatically, that makes looking up the exact call trivial.
[01:42] [small pause - screen flicker]
[01:48] Liam: opening a slow trace - this one has 2.3s latency, let's expand the waterfall. You'll see stages: routing, tokenization, model exec, post-processing. The model exec step has a long tail here.
[02:10] Omar: can you show the span ids and parent-child relationships? We need that for our tracing standard.
[02:16] Liam: yeah - each span is clickable; it shows span id, parent, start/end times, and logs attached. You can also export spans as .json for our tracing ingest.

[02:40] Liam: here's a useful thing - we surface model variant in the trace metadata. This one fell back to a 7B-quantized variant because the primary 13B was at capacity, so the tokenization + model exec timings differ.
[02:58] Rachel: fallback - that could explain some of the output drift we've seen. Is fallback policy configurable?
[03:05] Maya: yes, Routing Policies -> Model Fallbacks, you can set fallbacks per route with pinned versions or disable fallback for strict consistency.

[03:18] Liam: drilling into the model exec span, attached logs show a 'kv cache miss' spike and subsequent cold-start for the slice, that added ~600ms. You can see the request logs linked inline - click the "Request Log" icon.
[03:37] [typing noise]
[03:43] Liam: here's the raw request log entry - it includes request_id, user_id (redacted in UI for PII), model_version, token_count, and the backend node id. You can download or share a permalink for support.
[04:00] Sophia: how long are logs retained, and can we control retention per workspace?
[04:06] Maya: default retention is 90 days for hosted, but Dedicated/Private can set retention policies; plus we offer longer retention as an add-on. Audit logs are configurable and available via S3 export.

[04:26] Liam: next, error analysis. Under Observability -> Errors you get grouped error types by fingerprint. Common ones are 'model timeouts', 'model tokenization errors', 'toolcall parsing exceptions'.
[04:44] Rachel: we saw 'tokenization errors' in our pipeline that produce truncated outputs, is that what you call tokenization exceptions?
[04:52] Liam: yes often caused by mismatched tokenizer config when a variant is selected. The Console links the tokenizer version and shows a diff if there's a change between model versions.

[05:10] Liam: demoing a failing request now - open trace, click error badge, it shows stack-like trace with error logs. Look at this line: 'incompatible-tokenizer: unknown token ID at pos 143' and then a model fallback event prior to that.
[05:33] Omar: so the fallback selected a model with a different tokenizer embedding table - that's not great. Could we block fallback when tokenizer mismatch is detected?
[05:42] Liam: yes that's a policy we recommend - you can mark variants as incompatible for automatic fallback in the model catalog. We can also add a pre-flight check in your pipeline.

[05:56] Rachel: if we mark variants incompatible, what's the failover behavior? Will it queue or return a 503?
[06:03] Maya: you can choose - either hard-fail (503) or route to a higher-cost stable variant. Defaults to a graceful fallback but you can make it strict.

[06:20] Liam: switching to Request Logs view; this is a high-cardinality table with filterable columns. You can group by route, model, or response_code. Notice the 'linked trace' column which opens the trace view inline.
[06:38] Liam: I'll apply a filter for response_code=500 and sort by last_seen. Here are several entries, click one to open the payload inspector.
[06:46] [background chatter]
[06:50] Liam: payload inspector shows headers, prompt, model args, and a scrubbed copy of the response. We automatically mask likely PII fields but you can configure redaction rules.
[07:05] Sophia: can we plug our own redaction lambda or webhook?
[07:09] Liam: yes for Dedicated/Private you can run a custom processor in the pipeline or use the redact webhook to mutate logs before storage.

[07:25] Liam: ok showing correlation now - I search by our example request id Rachel sent earlier, 9b3c-... here it is. Trace shows a spike at t+0.9s for model exec and a downstream error at t+1.1s. The request log shows the full prompt and the response truncated.
[07:45] Rachel: that matches the customer complaint, thanks. Can we set up automated alerts for rate of tokenization errors?
[07:53] Liam: absolutely - Alerts -> create -> select 'error fingerprint' = tokenization exceptions -> set threshold. You can route alerts to PagerDuty or Slack.

[08:08] Omar: security question: how are these traces and request logs encrypted at rest?
[08:14] Maya: all data at rest is encrypted with AES-256. For Private/Dedicated we support BYOK via KMS/HSM and customer-managed keys. Audit logs are tamper-evident with signed digests.

[08:32] Liam: jumping deeper - I'm opening the node diagnostic for the backend host that handled the request. It shows GPU memory, kernel version, quantization profile, and the exact model binary hash. Since we saw a 7B quantized fallback, note the quantization profile differs and we can see the quantization error stats.
[08:54] Rachel: nice - can we get those stats exported so our model team can analyze accuracy drift?
[08:59] Liam: yes export to CSV or push to your metrics pipeline via our webhook.

[09:12] Liam: now a quick demo of root cause chaining: Console links traces with recent deployment events - here you see a rollout 10 minutes before the spike that upgraded a model variant on a subset of hosts. That correlates with the tokenization errors.
[09:31] Rachel: so a rollout caused a variant mismatch for a subset - we need guardrails.
[09:36] Maya: we recommend canary rollouts + rollout checks; Redwood can automatically abort rollouts when error rate exceeds threshold.

[09:48] Liam: next, show the replay feature - you can replay a request against a pinned model version in an isolated sandbox. This helps reproduce and verify fixes without impacting live traffic.
[10:02] Omar: is replayed data stored? We need it off by default.
[10:06] Liam: replay is ephemeral unless you choose to persist results; default ephemeral.

[10:18] Rachel: can we run a batch of replays - like 100 failing requests - in parallel?
[10:22] Liam: yes, Replay -> bulk upload -> choose target model -> concurrency limit. The console will show per-request success/failure and traces for each replay.

[10:38] [short tech detour about KV cache warm-up]
[10:44] Liam: earlier we saw cache misses; the Console shows cache-hit heatmaps by route and time window. You can configure pre-warming scripts for Dedicated.
[10:54] Rachel: do you have examples of pre-warm scripts?
[10:57] Liam: we have templates in the docs; I'll drop the link after the call.

[11:08] Maya: quick pause - any blocker on the pilot from Atlas side?
[11:12] Rachel: we need SOC2, network diagrams, and confirmation of retention controls. Also the security team will want SAML and SCIM for provisioning.
[11:22] Maya: noted, we'll send SOC2 and architecture diagrams today/tomorrow. We support SAML/SCIM and can demo SSO during pilot kickoff.

[11:33] Liam: back to error analysis - Console can surface aggregated impact: errors by user cohort or route, and estimated cost impact of retries. Useful for prioritizing fixes.
[11:48] Rachel: will the Console show per-token cost delta when falling back to a larger model?
[11:54] Liam: yes, cost estimation per trace, and recommended action (e.g., cache prefix, pin variant) with estimated $/1000 token savings.

[12:07] [noise - someone mutes/unmutes]
[12:14] Sophia: a compliance question - do you keep IPs in logs? Our legal team requires hashed IPs only.
[12:20] Maya: we can hash or remove IPs, support PII obfuscation rules - we will include the config examples.

[12:32] Liam: walking through a joint debugging flow: Rachel uploads a sample failing request id, we find it's a tokenizer mismatch after a canary, block fallback, replay request against 13B pinned, confirm output, then plan rollback.
[12:51] Rachel: that workflow sounds good. Will your SE help run the first two replays?
[12:56] Liam: yes we can run replays with you and monitor. We'll need the sample requests.

[13:06] Maya: quick recap of features shown: tracing waterfall with spans, linked request logs, error fingerprinting, model variant metadata, node diagnostics, replay/sandbox, RBAC/audit and redaction controls, and rollout guardrails.

[13:28] Rachel: great, last question - what SLAs are available for Dedicated?

[13:33] Maya: Dedicated offers uptime SLAs and latency p99 targets configurable per commitment tier. We'll attach the SLA doc in the follow-up.

[13:42] Omar: and pricing for pilot?

[13:45] Maya: we'll share a pilot pricing sheet and typical pilot scope (1-2 weeks benchmarking, small dedicated pool or hosted with committed capacity).

[13:54] Liam: ok I'll drop a couple of links in the chat: SOC2 creds, redaction docs, replay guide, and pre-warm templates.

[14:05] Maya: next steps - we'll send docs, run the benchmark, and schedule pilot kickoff. Who's the PM on your side?

[14:12] Rachel: that's me, I'll coordinate internal stakeholders.

[14:18] Maya: perfect. Thanks everyone.

[14:22] Omar: thanks, bye.

[14:24] [meeting ends]

Post-meeting notes: action items recorded above; Liam to also prepare a short benchmark config and include expected metrics to collect (latency p50/p95/p99, token throughput, error fingerprints). The team noted the tokenizer mismatch as the likely root cause and will treat model variant compatibility as a guardrail for rollout policies.
